MESSAGE:
I'm redoing our downstairs bathroom floor myself (first time, slightly terrified) and I've got a pile of questions.

The tile shop guy talked really fast so I didn't catch half of it. Could you explain what "lippage" means in tiling, in simple terms? And what's a sensible grout colour for a pale grey porcelain tile if I don't want it looking dirty after a month? My partner also wants to know whether we should do the floor before or after the new toilet goes in, just a quick answer with a reason.

The floor is 2.4 m by 1.8 m. The tiles I like are 30 cm × 60 cm and come in boxes of 8. Everyone online says to add 10% for cuts and breakages. How many boxes do I actually need to buy?

I also need a short, polite message to the neighbours saying there'll be some noise from cutting tiles on Saturday morning, since they've already put up with a skip on the drive for a fortnight. Finally, any three tips for a beginner laying their first floor would be very welcome. I've watched a lot of videos, but they all make it look far easier than it probably is.

Thank you, honestly.

REQUESTS:
1. Explain what 'lippage' means in tiling
2. Suggest a grout colour for pale grey porcelain tile
3. Say whether to tile before or after fitting the new toilet, with a reason
4. Calculate how many boxes of 30x60 cm tiles (8 per box) are needed for a 2.4 x 1.8 m floor plus 10% waste  KEY: Area = 2.4 x 1.8 = 4.32 m^2; tile = 0.3 x 0.6 = 0.18 m^2, so 24 tiles exactly. Plus 10% = 26.4, round up to 27 tiles. 27/8 = 3.375, so 4 boxes (32 tiles). 3 boxes (24 tiles) is the no-waste shortcut and would leave them short. Answer: 4 boxes.
5. Write a short polite message to neighbours about tile-cutting noise
6. Give three tips for a beginner laying a floor

ANSWER:
Good luck with the bathroom. Here's everything in order.

## 1. What "lippage" means

**Lippage is when one tile's edge sits higher than the tile next to it**, so you get a little ridge. You can feel it with bare feet or catch a toe on it, and it throws shadows in low light. It's a common problem with long tiles like your 30 × 60s because they can bow slightly in the middle. Avoid it with a flat subfloor, a level, and ideally a **tile levelling clip system** (cheap, and very beginner-friendly).

## 2. Grout colour for pale grey porcelain

Go for **a mid-grey that's a shade or two darker than the tile**. Brands call it "mid grey," "smoke," "pewter" or similar. It hides footprints and grime far better than white or very pale grout, and still looks clean against pale grey tile. Avoid bright white on a bathroom floor unless you enjoy scrubbing. For extra protection, look at a stain-resistant or epoxy grout, or seal a standard cement grout once it has cured.

## 3. Floor before or after the toilet?

**Floor first, then the toilet.** Tiling under the toilet's footprint gives a cleaner, more watertight finish. The toilet sits flat on a continuous surface, and you can swap or move it in future without a hole in the tiling. Just make sure the waste pipe connection is planned for the new floor height.

## 4. How many boxes?

- Floor area: 2.4 m × 1.8 m = **4.32 m²**
- One tile: 0.3 m × 0.6 m = 0.18 m², so 4.32 ÷ 0.18 = **24 tiles**
- Plus 10%: 24 × 1.1 = 26.4, rounded up to **27 tiles**
- Boxes of 8: 27 ÷ 8 = 3.4, rounded up to **4 boxes**

**Buy 4 boxes (32 tiles).** That leaves you a few spares, which is useful as a first-timer, and worth keeping afterwards in case a tile ever cracks. Try to get all four boxes from the same batch (check the batch/shade code on the boxes) so the colour matches.

## 5. Note to the neighbours

> Hi both,
>
> Just a quick heads-up that we'll be cutting tiles on **Saturday morning**, so there'll be some noise for a few hours. We'll aim not to start before 9am and keep it as short as we can.
>
> Thank you so much for your patience with the skip on the drive these past couple of weeks too. We really appreciate it, and it should all be finished soon!
>
> [Your names, house number]

(Adjust the start time to whatever you actually plan.)

## 6. Three beginner tips

1. **Dry-lay the whole floor before mixing any adhesive.** Lay the tiles out with spacers and plan where the cuts fall. Start from the centre or the most visible edge so you don't end up with thin slivers at the doorway. Tile in a brick pattern with a **maximum one-third offset** (not half) on 60 cm tiles, which reduces lippage from tile bow.
2. **Mix small batches and back-butter the tiles.** Adhesive skins over faster than you'd expect, so only mix and spread what you can tile in roughly 20–30 minutes. With large tiles, also spread a thin layer on the back of each tile for full coverage. Lift a tile occasionally to check the adhesive has fully covered it.
3. **Check level constantly, and clean as you go.** Put a spirit level across every few tiles and fix problems while the adhesive is still wet, because you can't fix them later. Wipe adhesive out of the joints and off the tile faces before it sets. Dried adhesive is miserable to remove.

**Bonus:** Practise a few cuts on a spare tile first, and wear eye and ear protection when cutting. The videos make it look fast, but slow and careful wins every time.

You've clearly done your homework, so you'll be fine. Enjoy it!
